relevance_note: Case report of an infant girl with a TNFAIP3 variant, also carried by her father and paternal uncle: "We identified a heterozygous variant in TNFAIP3, namely NM_006290.4:c.460G > T".
method_note: Single-case report with family history; no tables. All rows written by hand into a small Python builder script (in the private scratch directory) that copies every span from the paper text, so unusual spaces (thin spaces in 'c.460G > T', four-per-em spaces before units) are preserved. Individuals: the index patient plus six relatives named in the family-history and segregation paragraphs. 'brother of paternal grandfather' (died at 16) and 'father's uncle' (Crohn's disease) are listed separately in the paper and kept as two rows; they could be the same person, and the pedigree (Figure 9) is an image, not text. The father and uncle variant rows give the variant string from the abstract plus the sentence attributing 'the same' variant to them. For the uncle the paper says 'the same mutations' (plural), although only one TNFAIP3 variant is described. Zygosity was not recorded for the father or uncle because the paper states 'heterozygous' only for the index patient. The TNFRSF13B risk allele is recorded for the index patient and for the mother, from 'the maternal origin of the TNFRSF13B allele'. The mother's own zygosity is not stated. The mother's TNFAIP3 result is implied negative by 'paternal origin', but no variant row records that. n_patients_reported is null because the authors never state a count. They frame it as one patient, but three people carry the variant. cites_prior_report_of_same_patients is null because the paper says nothing either way. 'VES' (listed among normal first-level tests) was read as erythrocyte sedimentation rate; CRP was elevated at the same admission, so the checklist item 'elevated inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR)' is observed on CRP. Checklist decisions: 'diabetes' is reported only as a steroid side effect, so 'type 1 diabetes' is not reported. The anemia was attributed to gastrointestinal bleeding, so 'cytopenia (autoimmune)' is not reported. A single febrile episode is not 'recurrent fever'. Normal ASCA/ANCA do not exclude 'autoantibodies (ANA/other)'. Colonic lymphoid nodular hyperplasia (only 'suggestive of' on colonoscopy) was not counted as lymphoproliferation. The father's vitiligo was not counted as 'skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)'. The father's thyroiditis was counted as autoimmune thyroiditis because the paper lists it under 'autoimmune conditions'. The father's uncle's Crohn's disease was counted as gastrointestinal inflammation. Age at diagnosis and age at last evaluation are not stated; 'one-year-old' is the age at first presentation to the centre, so it was not used. No internal contradictions were found. One possible typo: adalimumab dose printed as '20 mg/kg every two weeks'; it is recorded as printed.
